how-much-to-charge-to-replace-a-well-pum.text:
← Well pump bid calculator

How much to charge to replace a well pump

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$1,495 well-pump special,” or a price they saw for a pump swap on a coupon site. That number is not a takeoff. A 60-foot 1/2 HP submersible with a pitless that comes apart is not the same job as a 280-foot 1.5 HP pull with a seized adapter, a stuck pump, 300 feet of well cable, a new tank, and a constant-pressure drive. The trip is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the extra footage and the pitless, not just the trip

Water-heater calculators price a vent, a gas upsize, and an attic. Septic-pumping calculators price a tank lid, a hose, and extra gallons. Hydro-jet calculators price a drain line and a toilet pull. Electrical-panel calculators price a feeder and a utility. A well-pump job is a well: the pump, the depth past the included footage, how the pitless comes apart, and the tank that keeps the well from short-cycling. Quoting all of that from a published special is how the first seized adapter eats the field margin.

A job with the same trip can cost much more

Each extra foot past the included run is time that never appears on the coupon. A seized pitless is billed as its own hours and an adapter. A stuck pump, extra well cable, a new tank, and a constant-pressure drive are adders that get forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a 280-foot 1.5 HP pull with a seized pitless, a stuck pump, 300 feet of cable, a new tank, and a VFD prices about $5,915 ($21 per foot of well depth, 13.5 crew-hours). The same shop’s 60-foot 1/2 HP pump-only swap prices about $1,176 ($20 per foot, 3.8 hours, walk-away $765). Matching the brochure job’s $1,495 special on the deep seized well is how that job becomes a loss — the walk-away on the deep job is already $3,845.

A jet-pump and tank job is not automatically the cheap one

A 40-foot jet pump with a new tank and no pitless is not the 60-foot submersible special minus 100%. On the sample rates that jet job prices about $1,585 ($40 per foot, 3.8 crew-hours) — similar hours to the brochure submersible, not because the jet is slower but because the tank does not live in a published pump-only special. A 120-foot 3/4 HP submersible with a new tank and a good pitless prices about $2,110 (5.2 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first seized adapter.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $42/h tech loaded at 32% payroll burden is $55.44. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a well-drilling specification, a water-quality report, a building-code determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Well depth, horsepower, tank size, pitless condition, and whether a constant-pressure drive is required are yours to confirm.

Price your well-pump job

Common questions

How much to charge to replace a well pump?

Charge from the trip, the pull (submersible versus jet), extra drop-pipe footage past the included run, horsepower, pitless condition, stuck-pump pull, extra well cable, a new pressure tank, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 60-foot 1/2 HP submersible swap that keeps the tank, at the sample rates in this calculator, prices around $1,176 — about $20 per foot of well depth.

Why is a $1,495 well-pump special dangerous?

Homeowners count the trip. Extra footage, a seized pitless, a stuck pump, extra cable, a new tank, and a constant-pressure drive do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper special written for a 60-foot 1/2 HP swap is how a 280-foot seized-pitless job becomes a half-day loss.

How much to charge to replace a well pump and pressure tank?

A pump-and-tank job is not a pump-only special. On the sample rates a 120-foot 3/4 HP submersible with a new tank and a good pitless prices around $2,110 ($18 per foot, 5.2 crew-hours), while a 60-foot 1/2 HP pump-only special prices around $1,176 ($20 per foot, 3.8 hours).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not plumbing, well-drilling, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a well-drilling specification, or a water-quality report — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      Why does a 120-foot well only bill 20 feet of extra footage?

      Because the base pump price already carries the first 100 feet of setting depth. The default well is 120 ft, so only the 20 ft past the allowance is charged as extra footage. The “included footage” field is there so you can match it to how your own supplier or price book bundles depth — set it to zero and every foot bills separately.

      Why is cable measured separately from well depth?

      Because the cable run is longer than the well is deep. It has to reach from the pump up past the pitless adapter and across to the pressure tank or control box, so the default is 130 ft of cable for a 120 ft well. With 100 ft included, that is 30 extra feet at $1.85, or $55.50. Under-measuring the cable is a common way a well job goes over: the hole depth is known, the horizontal run to the tank often is not until you are on site.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit, a share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your well depth, wages, or prices.

      Why is the effective hourly rate $408 when I set my wage at $42?

      Because most of this job is not labor. The default takes 5.17 hours and prices at $2,109.70, so dividing one by the other gives $408.07 an hour — but $790.50 of that price is material (the pump, tank, cable, and hoist), which is 57.6% of direct cost against labor’s 20.9%. The effective hourly figure is useful for comparing how well your day is being bought, not as a rate to quote.

      What is the $75 hoist line for?

      Pulling and setting a submersible pump on a 120-foot string is not a hand operation. The hoist line covers the rig or tripod time attributable to this job rather than the crew hours, which are counted separately. If you own the hoist outright and would rather carry it in your overhead rate, set the field to zero — it is a plain pass-through, not a percentage.

vs-a-flat-well-pump-special.html.text:
← Well Pump Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $1,495 well-pump special

“We install a well pump for $1,495” is not a price for a well — it is a price for one specific depth, pitless condition, and scope, quietly applied to every well that calls in.

What a flat well-pump special is

A flat well-pump price is the fastest way to quote: one number, easy to advertise and easy for a homeowner to compare between bids. It is the number a homeowner holding a flyer or a Facebook special will call and ask you to match, whatever their well actually needs.

The number behind it was set for one job — a shallow well, a pitless adapter that comes apart cleanly, no stuck pump, and the existing tank kept — and then reused for every well afterward, whether or not the next job looks anything like the one the special was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the well depth past the included footage, pump type and horsepower, whether the pitless adapter is free or seized, a stuck-pump pull, extra well cable, a pressure-tank replacement, and a constant-pressure drive, plus your own labor hours and material costs. It prices the depth, the pitless, and every extra separately by kind, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this well, not a generic one.

What a flat well-pump special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same flat number whether the well is 60 feet or 280 feet, even though extra depth past the included footage does not bill itself. Prices extra drop-pipe footage separately at your own hours-per-foot rate, so a deep well costs more than a shallow one.
Has no line for the pitless adapter, regardless of whether it comes apart cleanly or is seized and has to be replaced. Prices pitless-replacement hours and fittings separately by condition, so a seized pitless costs more than a free one.
Has no line for a stuck pump, extra well cable, or a pressure-tank replacement, regardless of how many the job needs. Prices each extra separately — a stuck pull, cable past the included run, the tank, and a constant-pressure drive — so a fully loaded job costs more than a bare swap.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against a flat special, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two wells, the same depth-blind special

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($42/hr crew wage, 32% burden, 18% overhead, a 35% target margin):

JobThis calculator's priceThe flat $1,495 specialGap
60 ft 1/2 HP submersible, good pitless, keep the existing tank — the job the $1,495 special is built on$1,176.19 bid price; $764.52 break-even cost$1,495.00The special actually prices $318.81 above the calculator's own bid on this job.
280 ft 1.5 HP, seized pitless, stuck pump, new tank, extra cable, constant-pressure drive$5,915.32 bid price; $3,844.96 break-even cost$1,495.00The special quotes $2,349.96 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $4,420.32 below the calculator's own bid price.

The flat special is a fixed $1,495, not derived from either job. On the shallow well it is generous; on the deep, seized-pitless, stuck-pump job it is a loss before a dollar of labor gets paid. Run your own well's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one well it was built for, and nothing about a flat number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat special skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat well-pump special get a bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is depth past the included footage, whether the pitless adapter comes apart or has to be replaced, a stuck pump, extra cable, a new tank, and a constant-pressure drive -- not "a well pump." A 280-foot 1.5 HP pull with a seized pitless, a stuck pump, a new tank, extra cable, and a VFD is doing several jobs a 60-foot 1/2 HP swap with a good pitless and the existing tank never touches, none of which a flat special's single number can see.

What does a flat well-pump special usually leave out entirely?

Footage past the price's included depth, whether the pitless is free or seized, a stuck-pump pull, extra well cable beyond what a shallow well needs, a pressure tank replacement, and a constant-pressure drive. A shallow well with an easy pitless and no tank swap is doing far less than a deep well needing all of the above -- and a flat number has no line for any of it.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates: a 60-foot 1/2 HP submersible swap with a good pitless and the existing tank -- the job the $1,495 brochure special is built on -- prices at $1,176.19, with a $764.52 break-even cost. A 280-foot 1.5 HP pull with a seized pitless, a stuck pump, a new tank, extra cable, and a constant-pressure drive prices at $5,915.32, with a $3,844.96 break-even cost. Quoting that second job at the flat $1,495 special prices it $2,349.96 below its own break-even cost -- before a dollar of profit -- and $4,420.32 below the calculator's own bid price.

Is a flat well-pump special ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- shallow depth, a good pitless, no stuck pump, the existing tank kept -- a flat rate can land close, and on this calculator's own easy preset the flat special actually prices above the calculator's own bid. The risk is applying the same number outside that band without noticing, because the flat rate does not know which well it was priced for and neither does the estimator until depth, pitless condition, and extras are actually spelled out.

Does this calculator know what materials or labor cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates. It takes the well's depth, pump type and horsepower, pitless condition, stuck-pump pull, extra cable, tank, and constant-pressure drive, plus the labor hours and material costs you enter, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat special skips, not a market survey.

No warranty. This calculator vs. ServiceTitan

Two different shapes: ServiceTitan is an account-based field service management platform for running a well-service or plumbing company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one well-pump job cost, given its depth and its extras, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan, headquartered in Glendale, California. It serves HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and other trades with scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, reporting, and job costing across a whole business, with a mobile app for crews in the field. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across a whole company, not a one-off calculator. ServiceTitan's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — field service management software serving HVAC and plumbing among other trades, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceTitan appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceTitan does. It does not schedule techs, dispatch crews, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one well-pump job's setting depth past the included run, submersible-versus-jet hours, pump horsepower, a good versus a seized pitless adapter, a stuck-pump pull, extra well cable past the included run, a new pressure tank, and a constant-pressure drive, plus your crew wage, payroll burden, travel, overhead, and target margin. It turns that into the price, the price per foot of depth, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Should I use this calculator or ServiceTitan?

They do different jobs, and a well-service or plumbing shop of any size will likely end up touching both eventually.
